  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Cutting documents into chunks}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A model reads a long document in pieces, called *chunks*, and chunking decides
what it can see together. A figure in one chunk and the sentence that explains
it in the next may never be read side by side. This guide covers the nine ways
harnessr cuts a document, the settings every one of them shares, and how to
compare chunkings before you pay for any reading.

Six of the nine segmenters make no model calls, and a seventh makes none by
default, so you can try them for nothing. `vignette("harnessr")` introduces the
package and the ideas used here, and `vignette("ingest")` covers the step before
this one.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")
```

`embedder = "lexical"` makes the one segmenter that embeds text, `semantic`, use
hashed bag-of-words vectors rather than an embeddings endpoint, so this guide
runs offline and gives the same chunks every time.

## What segmentation produces

`gr_segment()` takes a document from `gr_ingest()` (or anything `gr_ingest()`
accepts) and a segmentation, and returns a chunk set:

```{r}
doc <- gr_ingest(gr_example())
ch <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
ch
```

The segmentation can be a segmenter's name, a named list as above, or a
`gr_segment_spec()`. Each chunk records where it came from:

```{r}
ch$chunks[, c("chunk_id", "tokens", "page", "section", "block_id")]
```

`page` is `NA` here because the example is Markdown, which has no pages; a PDF
fills it in. `block_id` is `NA` on a chunk built from several blocks, and so is
`page` on a chunk that runs from one page onto the next. A chunk that is not
from one place says so rather than naming the first place it touches. This
provenance is what `ans$evidence` reports for every chunk an answer rests on.

You rarely call `gr_segment()` yourself. `answer_document()` does it, using the
`segment` part of a recipe:

```{r}
gr_recipe("survey")$segment[c("method", "max_tokens", "overlap_tokens")]
```

To change it, build a recipe of your own with
`gr_recipe(segment = list(...))`; `vignette("readers")` covers recipes.

## The nine segmenters

Each segmenter is a different hypothesis about where meaning breaks:

| segmenter | boundary hypothesis | cost | needs client | provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | meaning is uniform; cut on a ruler (the control condition) | free | no | none |
| `paragraph` | the author's paragraph breaks are real | free | no | page, section, block |
| `sentence` | sentences are atomic; pack tightly | free | no | page, section, block |
| `recursive` | use the strongest separator that still fits | free | no | none |
| `structural` | headings are boundaries; never merge across sections | free | no | page, section, block |
| `page` | the page is the unit: forms, invoices, scanned records | free | no | page, section, block |
| `semantic` | cut where consecutive embeddings diverge most | 1 embedding pass | yes | page, section, block |
| `contextual` | chunks prefixed with where they sit | free, or 1 call/chunk | only for `context_source = "llm"` | page, section, block |
| `proposition` | rewrite into standalone factual statements | 1 call per ~900-token batch | yes | none |

The cost and client columns come from the registry, so you can check them
rather than trust them:

```{r}
gr_segmenters()[, c("name", "cost", "needs_client", "calls")]
```

`paragraph` is the default. It packs the author's paragraphs, in order, into
chunks up to the cap. `sentence` packs sentences instead, which gives more,
smaller chunks with cleaner edges. `structural` never lets a chunk cross a
heading, and by default (`prefix_section = TRUE`) starts every chunk with its
section's heading, so the fourth chunk of a long "Methods" section still says it
is about methods. When the extractor found no sections, `structural` finds
headings itself: a Markdown `#` line, or a short line that is numbered or
written in capitals. `page` makes one chunk per page, splitting only a page too
long for the cap, and says so when it does.

`fixed` cuts the text into windows of equal size and ignores its structure,
which makes it the baseline to measure the others against. `recursive` splits on
the strongest separator that still gives pieces under the cap: by default blank
lines, then line breaks, then sentence ends, semicolons, commas and spaces. Set
your own cascade, strongest first, with `separators`.

`fixed` and `recursive` work on the whole document joined into one string, by
design, so their chunks carry no page or section. That is the cost of ignoring
structure, and it is reported as `NA` rather than guessed at:

```{r}
fx <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "fixed", max_tokens = 120))
fx$chunks[1:3, c("chunk_id", "page", "section", "block_id")]
```

The last three segmenters, `semantic`, `contextual` and `proposition`, are
covered below, under the settings and model calls they add.

## When a segmenter cannot run as asked

A segmenter that cannot do what was asked falls back to one that can, warns,
and records the change. `page` on a source with no page numbers falls back to
`paragraph`:

```{r warning = FALSE}
pg <- gr_segment(doc, "page")
pg$method
```

`semantic` without a client falls back to `paragraph`, and `proposition`
without one falls back to `sentence`. The fallback shows in `$method`
(`"semantic->paragraph"`, `"proposition->sentence"`) and in the `method` column
of `gr_chunk_stats()`, so a comparison never reports a chunking that did not
run. `contextual` keeps its name when `context_source = "llm"` has no client,
because only the source of its context lines changed; `$extra$context_source`
records `"metadata"`, the one that ran.

Every one of these warnings has the class `gr_segment_fallback`, and it is
carried onto the answer of any read that uses the chunks.

## Chunk size

`max_tokens` is the cap on a chunk's size, and every segmenter is held to it,
including one you register yourself. After a segmenter returns, `gr_segment()`
splits any chunk over the cap (at sentences, then words, then characters) and
counts how many it had to split in `$extra$cap_enforced`. The pieces keep the
page, section and block of the chunk they came from. If the active tokenizer
counts a single character as more than the cap, `gr_segment()` stops with an
error of class `gr_cap_unenforceable` rather than send a chunk the model will
reject.

A setting out of range is corrected and the correction is announced:

```{r}
tryCatch(gr_segment_spec("paragraph", max_tokens = 100, overlap_tokens = 500),
         warning = conditionMessage)
```

`max_tokens` is held to between 32 and 1,000,000, `overlap_tokens` to less than
`max_tokens`, and `min_tokens` to no more than `max_tokens`.

What the right size is depends on the reader. A reader that sends every chunk
pays for each request, so small chunks multiply the bill; one that picks the
best few chunks needs chunks small enough that the best few hold the answer and
little else. `vignette("readers")` compares them.

## Overlap

Without overlap, an answer that straddles a boundary is split between two
chunks and may be lost by both. `overlap_tokens` copies the end of each chunk
into the start of the next. It costs duplicated tokens, which
`gr_chunk_stats()` shows as a larger `total_tokens`:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30, 60), function(ov)
  gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 120,
                                      overlap_tokens = ov)))))
```

The document is the same 534 tokens each time: at 60 tokens of overlap the
model would be sent 863, about 60% more. The carried text is cut at a sentence
boundary when one is close, otherwise at a word; text written without spaces
(Chinese, Japanese, Thai) is cut by characters. The overlap is trimmed so that
the chunk it opens still fits the cap.

Provenance counts the overlap. A chunk that opens with a sentence carried from
page 3 and goes on to page 4 reports page `NA`, since it is not wholly from
either.

Overlap applies to every segmenter except `page`, where the page is the unit,
and `proposition`, whose statements are written to stand alone, so its overlap
is always 0. `structural` applies it within a section, never across a heading.

## Minimum size

`min_tokens` merges a chunk smaller than this into the chunk before it, so a
one-line paragraph between two headings does not become a request of its own.
The merge happens only when the result still fits the cap. With a cap of 60
tokens the example's paragraphs give fourteen chunks, the smallest of 8 tokens;
`min_tokens = 30` folds one of them away:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30), function(m)
  gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 60,
                                      min_tokens = m)))))
```

`fixed` and `page` ignore `min_tokens`. `structural` applies it within a
section only, because it never merges across headings: its 16-token first
chunk, the report's title, stays as it is whatever you set.

```{r}
gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                    min_tokens = 40)))
```

## Context lines

A chunk retrieved on its own can be hard to place: "it rose 17 percent" means
little without the section it came from. `contextual` packs paragraphs as
`paragraph` does, then starts each chunk with a bracketed line saying where it
sits. By default (`context_source = "metadata"`) the line is built from the
file name, section, page and position, for nothing:

```{r}
ctx <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "contextual", max_tokens = 120))
cat(ctx$chunks$text[2])
```

With `context_source = "llm"` a model writes the line instead, one call per
chunk, from the chunk, the document's first 1,500 tokens and the chunk's
section path from the document's headings (`"Report > Results"`), so a chunk
from deep in a long document can be placed. It makes one request per chunk and
never more: `$extra$cost` declares `calls` and `calls_max` as the number of
chunks. The mock client below stands in for that model:

```{r}
writer <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "This excerpt reports the 2024 results.")
ctx_llm <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "contextual", max_tokens = 120,
                                context_source = "llm"), client = writer)
cat(ctx_llm$chunks$text[2])
```

Room for the line is held back from each chunk before packing (90 tokens for
`"llm"`, the longest header the document could need for `"metadata"`, never
more than half of `max_tokens`), so adding the line never pushes a chunk over
the cap. A line that still does not fit is shortened; the document text is
not.

When a context call fails or is skipped at the run's limits, the chunk keeps
its text without a line. `$extra$blurbs_missing` counts those chunks, and a
`gr_segment_fallback` warning says so.

The context line is not the document's text, and a model may have written it.
So the chunk also keeps its body alone in a `source_text` column, and a
quotation from the chunk is checked against that, never against the line:

```{r}
ctx_llm$chunks$source_text[2]
unlist(ctx_llm$extra$cost)
```

## Segmenters that call a model

Three segmenters spend something, and each takes a `client`:

- `semantic` embeds the text a few sentences at a time (`semantic_window`,
  default 2) and cuts where two neighbouring windows differ most: at distances
  above the `semantic_percentile` (default 90; higher gives fewer, larger
  chunks), or, with `semantic_threshold = "texttiling"`, at the deep valleys
  of the similarity between neighbouring windows (see below). The packer then
  holds the pieces to the cap and the minimum.
- `contextual` with `context_source = "llm"` makes one call per chunk, as above.
- `proposition` sends the document in batches of about
  `proposition_batch_tokens` (default 900) and has the model rewrite each into
  standalone factual statements, with pronouns resolved and numbers kept as
  written. With `proposition_context_tokens` above 0, each batch's request
  also carries that many tokens from the end of the batch before it, so what
  it refers back to can be resolved. Its chunks are the model's words,
  so `source_text` holds the passage each was written from, and quotes are
  checked against that; each chunk keeps the page and section of its passage.
  A proposition with no support in its passage (a number the passage does not
  give, or most of its words absent) is counted in
  `$extra$propositions_unsupported`; with `proposition_check = "drop"` it is
  also dropped as invented, counted in `$extra$propositions_dropped`, with a
  `gr_proposition_dropped` warning. A
  batch that cannot be rewritten is kept as written rather than dropped, with
  a warning, and counted in `$extra$batches_kept_as_written`.

```{r}
cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "unused")
sem <- gr_segment(doc, list(method = "semantic", max_tokens = 120), client = cl)
gr_chunk_stats(sem)
sem$extra$embedding_source
```

`embedding_source` is `"lexical"` here, so the boundaries reflect shared words,
not meaning, and `$method` says so: `"semantic->lexical"`. With a real
embeddings endpoint it is `"api"`, and the method is `"semantic"`. The label
is all that differs; the chunks and the requests are the same.

These requests count against the run's limits, `hr_options(max_calls =,
max_cost_usd =)`, like any other. Called without a `trace`, `gr_segment()`
makes its own and returns it as `$trace`, so you can see what segmenting cost:

```{r}
hr_trace_summary(ctx_llm$trace)[, c("calls", "tokens_in", "tokens_out")]
```

`vignette("runs")` covers limits and traces.

## Comparing segmentations

`gr_chunk_stats()` sums a chunk set up in one row, so comparing chunkings is an
`rbind()`:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c("fixed", "paragraph", "sentence", "structural"),
  function(m) gr_chunk_stats(gr_segment(doc, list(method = m, max_tokens = 120)))))
```

`n` is the number of chunks, which is the number of requests for a reader that
sends every chunk. `total_tokens` grows with overlap and with text a segmenter
adds, such as the headings `structural` puts at the top of its chunks.
`over_cap` is 0 for anything `gr_segment()` returns, since the cap is enforced;
it is there for chunk sets built some other way. `method` names any fallback.

To compare what different chunkings do to an answer, give `gr_compare()`
recipes that differ only in their `segment`. It extracts the document once and
reuses a segmentation across recipes whose segment settings match, so only the
reading is paid for more than once:

```{r}
cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", list(
  gr_recipe("by_paragraph", segment = list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2)),
  gr_recipe("by_section", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2))), client = cl)
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "segmenter", "chunks", "reader", "chunks_used")]
```

## Choosing the settings

Each walkthrough below takes one segmentation setting or group: what it
controls and what it trades off, the signs in your results that point to
changing it, where its default came from, and how to test a change.
`vignette("settings")` lists every segmentation setting with its default.

The free statistics above (`gr_chunk_stats()`, and `gr_seg_recall()` and
`gr_seg_pk()` in `vignette("compare")`) are the first test of a chunking, since
they cost nothing. What a chunking does to answers is tested with arms:
`hr_sweep()` builds one arm per value and `hr_benchmark()` runs them on a
reference. Here the arms run on one question and a stand-in model that always
answers correctly, so the examples show how a sweep is built and read, not
which value is better. `vignette("compare")` runs a grid of segmenters and
chunk sizes on dev, then compares one choice on test with intervals.

```{r}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
says <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
sweep <- function(arms) {
  hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = says, split = "dev",
               scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
}
```

### Which segmenter {#set-method}

**What it controls.** `method` is where the cuts fall: on a ruler (`fixed`), at
the author's paragraphs, sentences or headings, at pages, or where the
embeddings shift (`semantic`). Each is a guess about where meaning breaks. A
cut through the middle of a table or an argument separates the parts a model
needs together; chunks that keep whole sections are larger and fewer.

**Signs it needs changing.** An answer that gives half a figure, or a quotation
that stops mid-sentence, points to cuts in the wrong places: look at the chunks
around it with `chunks$chunks$text`. `gr_seg_recall()` reporting the answer
outside the top chunks for one segmenter and inside for another is the same
sign, measured. A document with headings that a `paragraph` chunking runs
across is a candidate for `structural`; a form or invoice for `page`.

**Where the default came from.** `paragraph` was chosen because it needs no
model or embedder; it has not been compared with the others (`untested`).
Each recipe sets its own: `"needle"` uses `semantic`, `"precise"` uses
`sentence`.

**How to test it.** Sweep it on the recipe you use:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"),
                        list(method = c("paragraph", "sentence", "structural"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.method, bench, mean)
```

All three sent different requests here (`hr_sweep_check(bench)` has no rows),
and `structural` sent the most, 690 prompt tokens against 667 for `sentence`,
because its chunks carry their headings.

### Chunk size: `max_tokens` {#set-max-tokens}

**What it controls.** `max_tokens` caps every chunk. Smaller chunks make more
requests for a reader that sends every chunk, and let a reader that picks the
best few send less text around the answer; larger chunks keep more context
together and cost fewer requests.

**Signs it needs changing.** Under `map_reduce` or `skim`, a cost dominated by
the number of requests (`hr_trace_summary()`) points to larger chunks. Under
`retrieve`, an answer that is right but rests on long chunks of unrelated
text points to smaller ones, and an answer split across two chunks, of which
only one was picked, points to larger ones or to overlap.

**Where the default came from.** 1200 tokens was set when the segmenters were
written and not tuned (`untested`). The recipes set their own, from 500
(`"needle"`) to 4000 (`"fast"`).

**How to test it.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"), list(max_tokens = c(100, 200, 500))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.max_tokens, bench, mean)
```

Under `retrieve`, smaller chunks sent more here, 829 prompt tokens at 100
against 676 at 500. At 100 the report became eight chunks holding 704 tokens,
since each repeats the recipe's 50 tokens of overlap, and `retrieve` sent all
eight (the recipe's `top_k` is 8); at 500 it became two chunks of 563
tokens. Whether the answers
change is what a benchmark on your own reference measures.

### Overlap: `overlap_tokens` {#set-overlap}

**What it controls.** `overlap_tokens` copies the end of each chunk into the
start of the next, so a sentence near a cut is whole in at least one chunk. It
costs duplicated tokens in every request that carries both chunks, and for a
reader that sends every chunk, in every request (see "Overlap" above).

**Signs it needs changing.** An answer that needs the end of one chunk and the
start of the next, such as a figure in one and its unit in the other, points to
more overlap. A bill that grew with no change in answers points to less.

**Where the default came from.** 0, so no text is sent twice; it has not been
compared with other values (`untested`). Several recipes set 10% of their
chunk size.

**How to test it.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle", list(max_tokens = 100)),
                        list(overlap_tokens = c(0, 20, 50))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.overlap_tokens, bench, mean)
```

At 100-token chunks, 50 tokens of overlap sent 24% more prompt tokens than
none (829 against 669).

### Packing: `packing`, `min_tokens` and `runt_merge` {#set-packing}

**What they control.** How units (paragraphs, sentences, pieces) are packed
into chunks under the cap. `packing = "greedy"` fills each chunk to
`max_tokens` and leaves the remainder in the last chunk; `"balanced"` keeps
the same number of chunks and evens their sizes. `min_tokens` merges a chunk
smaller than it into the chunk before it; `runt_merge = "both"` also merges
a first chunk smaller than it forward into the second, which the backward
rule cannot reach, since nothing comes before it.

**Signs they need changing.** A last chunk much smaller than the others, in
a reader that weighs chunks alike (`retrieve` scoring, `map_reduce` notes),
points to `"balanced"`. A document whose first chunk is only its title, sent
as a request of its own, points to `min_tokens` with `runt_merge = "both"`.

**Where the defaults came from.** `"greedy"`, `min_tokens = 0` and
`"backward"` are how chunks were packed before these settings existed; none
has been compared with the alternatives (`untested`).

**How to test them.** The chunk sizes show what they do, for nothing:

```{r}
paras <- sprintf("Paragraph %02d reports the year's results in some detail, %s.", 1:25,
                 "with a few more words to give it some length")
long_doc <- gr_ingest(paste(c("Annual review", paras), collapse = "\n\n"))
sizes <- function(...) gr_segment(long_doc, gr_segment_spec("paragraph", ...))$chunks$tokens
sizes(max_tokens = 300)
sizes(max_tokens = 300, packing = "balanced")
```

Greedy packing leaves 197 tokens in the last of three chunks; balanced packing
makes three of 229, 252 and 225. What they do to answers is tested with arms:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle", list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 150)),
                        list(packing = c("greedy", "balanced"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.packing, bench, mean)
```

The two sent different requests here, 901 prompt tokens for `"balanced"`
against 876 for `"greedy"`, because `retrieve` picked chunks of different
sizes; whether answers change is what a benchmark on your own reference
measures.

### Semantic boundaries: `semantic_threshold` {#set-semantic}

**What it controls.** How `semantic` turns the distances between neighbouring
windows into cuts. `"percentile"` cuts every gap whose distance reaches the
`semantic_percentile` of them all, so about one gap in ten is cut whether the
text changes topic or not. `"texttiling"` cuts by depth score, the rule of
TextTiling (Hearst 1997): it compares the `semantic_window` sentences before
each gap with those after it, finds the valleys of that similarity, and cuts
a valley only when it is deep, both by Hearst's cutoff and by being deeper
than the similarities spread. A text on one topic then gets at most about one
cut, and a change of topic gets one. It uses the same embeddings, so it sends
the same requests.

**Signs it needs changing.** Under `semantic`, chunks that end in the middle
of an argument on a page with no change of subject point to `"texttiling"`.
A long document whose sections run together into a few large chunks under
`"texttiling"` points back to `"percentile"`.

**Where the default came from.** `"percentile"` is the rule `semantic` was
written with; it has not been compared with `"texttiling"` (`untested`).

**How to test it.** It sends the same embedding request either way, so the
first test is free: count the cuts.

```{r}
by_rule <- sapply(c("percentile", "texttiling"), function(rule) {
  gr_segment(doc, gr_segment_spec("semantic", max_tokens = 1200,
                                  semantic_threshold = rule), client = cl)$extra$boundaries
})
by_rule
```

The example report has a few short sections, and `"texttiling"` cuts it
twice where `"percentile"` cuts it three times. What the cuts do to answers is
tested with arms:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"),
                        list(semantic_threshold = c("percentile", "texttiling"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.semantic_threshold, bench, mean)
```

Under `"needle"`, whose chunks are at most 500 tokens, the two sent nearly the
same prompt tokens here (676 and 675): the packer, not the boundaries, sets
most of each chunk's size.

### Tables: `table_packing` {#set-tables}

**What it controls.** How `paragraph` packs the rows of a table. `"rows"`
packs them as it packs any other blocks, so a long table is cut wherever the
cap falls and only its first chunk carries the header row. `"grouped"` packs
each table on its own and opens every chunk of it with the header row, then
as many rows as fit. Either way, a document's blocks and the chunks of a
document with a table say which table and which rows they hold (`table_id`
and `table_rows`); that is provenance only and adds nothing to the text.

**Signs it needs changing.** Answers that read a figure from the wrong column
of a long table, or that cannot say what a row's numbers are, point to
`"grouped"`, so every chunk of rows says what its columns are. Many small
tables, each smaller than a chunk, gain nothing from it.

**Where the default came from.** `"rows"` is how tables were packed before
the setting existed; it has not been compared with `"grouped"` (`untested`).

**How to test it.** The chunks show what it does, for nothing:

```{r}
tab <- tempfile(fileext = ".md")
writeLines(c("# Sales by region", "",
             "| region | units | revenue |", "|---|---|---|",
             sprintf("| region %02d | %d | %d |", 1:30, 100 + 1:30, 1000 + 7 * 1:30)), tab)
tab_doc <- gr_ingest(tab)
by_packing <- lapply(c(rows = "rows", grouped = "grouped"), function(p) {
  gr_segment(tab_doc, gr_segment_spec("paragraph", max_tokens = 150, table_packing = p))
})
lapply(by_packing, function(ch) ch$chunks[, c("chunk_id", "tokens", "table_id", "table_rows")])
sapply(by_packing, function(ch) sum(startsWith(ch$chunks$text, "| region | units |")))
```

Under `"rows"` the table, which Markdown gives as one block, is packed after
the heading and cut wherever the cap falls, so no chunk opens with the header
row and each piece reports the rows of the whole block, `"1-31"`. Under
`"grouped"` every chunk of rows opens with the header, and `table_rows` says
which rows each holds. A table from Word or HTML comes one row per block, and
then `"rows"` gives each chunk its own range too. What it
does to answers is tested with arms on a reference whose documents have
tables, with `my_tables` that reference and `my_client` your client:

```{r eval = FALSE}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "paragraph")),
                 list(table_packing = c("rows", "grouped")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_tables, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
hr_report(bench)
```

### Context lines and propositions: `contextual` and `proposition` {#set-contextual}

**What they control.** `contextual` starts each chunk with a line saying where
it sits, built from the file's metadata for nothing, or written by a model
with `context_source = "llm"` (one request per chunk, capped at
`context_reply_tokens`, from the first `context_document_tokens` of the
document). `proposition` has a model rewrite the text into standalone
statements, one request per `proposition_batch_tokens` of text. Both help a
chunk retrieved on its own to make sense; both put words in the chunk that are
not the document's, which is why quotations are checked against
`source_text`.

**Signs they are needed.** Answers that confuse two sections that say similar
things ("revenue rose" in the 2023 and the 2024 section), or retrieval that
picks a chunk whose subject is a pronoun, point to `contextual`. Dense factual
text where each sentence leans on the one before points to `proposition`. A
segmentation bill that is a large share of the run (`ctx$trace`) points away
from the model-written versions.

**Where the defaults came from.** `context_source = "metadata"` was chosen as
the source that makes no request, and has not been compared with `"llm"`.
The section path `"llm"` sends and the test that finds an invented
proposition (every number in the passage, half its words in the passage or
its context) were set when they were written; neither was tuned.
`proposition_check = "count"` keeps every proposition, and
`proposition_context_tokens = 0` sends each batch alone, as before; neither
has been compared with the alternatives.
`proposition_batch_tokens` (900), `context_reply_tokens` (90),
`context_document_tokens` (1500) and `proposition_reply_tokens` (2000) are the
values the code had as constants; none was tuned (`untested`).

**How to test them.** Compare `contextual` with the segmenter it builds on:

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle", list(max_tokens = 100)),
                        list(method = c("paragraph", "contextual"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.method, bench, mean)
```

`contextual` sent 81 fewer prompt tokens here. The room it holds back for its
lines makes its chunks smaller, 73 tokens on average against 81, and the
recipe's eight chunks then hold less text.
`proposition` and `context_source = "llm"` need a model that writes real
statements, so they run on your own reference and client:

```{r eval = FALSE}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("needle"), data.frame(
  method = c("paragraph", "contextual", "contextual", "proposition"),
  context_source = c("metadata", "metadata", "llm", "metadata")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_reference, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(cbind(correct, usd) ~ param.method + param.context_source, bench, mean)
```

`proposition_check = "drop"` changes no request, only which propositions are
kept, so `$extra$propositions_unsupported` on one segmentation shows what it
would drop before you sweep it.

`context_source` is stored in the recipe even under a segmenter that ignores
it, so give it the value the other rows use for every row where it does
nothing, as above; a row that changes nothing else would otherwise be a second
arm sending the same requests, which `hr_sweep_check()` would then report.

## Previewing chunks in the Shiny app

The bundled app has a control for every segmentation setting: segmenter,
`max_tokens`, overlap and minimum chunk size. Its "Preview chunking" button shows
how the current settings cut the document before anything is spent on reading.
For a segmenter that calls a model, the button says so.

```{r eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "harnessr"))
```

`GPTREAD_DOC_ROOTS` (colon-separated) sets which folders the app can read.
Unset, it defaults to `~/Documents`, falling back to your entire home directory,
so set it before exposing the app to anyone else. The app opens only the PDF,
Word, text, Markdown, HTML and image files under those folders, never hidden
files or hidden folders. `extract` and `screen` are not offered, since they read
against a protocol; use `gr_extract()` and `gr_screen()` (`vignette("review")`).
A blank cost cap leaves `hr_options("max_cost_usd")` in force rather than
lifting the limit.

## Your own segmenter

`gr_register_segmenter()` adds a segmenter that behaves like the built-ins: it
appears in `gr_segmenters()`, can be named in a recipe, and is held to the same
cap. `new_chunks()` builds the object it must return. `vignette("extending")`
has a worked example.

```{r include = FALSE}
hr_options(old)
```
